title: Heartlight Adventures
note: Authored sample. Writing in the storybook stays in the page only and is not stored. Fictional demonstrations, not evidence of improved grades, clinical anxiety reduction, or guaranteed safety.

stories.title: The Gate of Sixes
stories.explore: Different strategies can reach the same answer.
stories.voice: I rushed. Your turn to choose our strategy.
stories.question: The gate shows four constellations, and each one holds six stars. How many stars is that?

choices.label: Count in sixes
choices.note: Start at six, then add another six, and keep the beat: six, twelve, eighteen…

choices.label: Draw the groups
choices.note: Four little clusters. Count one cluster, then the next, until the sky is counted.

choices.label: Split six into five and one
choices.note: Each constellation is five stars and one more. Gather the fives, then the ones.

stories.reveal: All three paths land on twenty-four. Counting in sixes goes 6, 12, 18, 24. Four drawn groups of six are the same stars. Splitting them makes four fives (20) and four ones (4), and 20 + 4 is 24. Questlight’s glow is for checking the work together — not for pretending Lumo knew it the first time.
stories.activity: Find four groups of six small things, like buttons, blocks or pebbles. Count them in sixes, as groups, and as fives-and-ones. See the same total arrive three ways.
stories.grownup: Lumo admits a rushed guess, then hands the strategy to the child. Praise the check, not the speed. Offer a pause if the counting feels heavy. This is a story about cooperating with a problem, not evidence of better marks.
stories.write: Which strategy would you try first, and why?

stories.title: The Save-Point Bridge
stories.explore: Stopping can be part of the plan.
stories.voice: Save point. We can stop, and the quest will wait.
stories.question: The star bridge is longer than it looked. What should the crew do?

choices.label: Rest at the lantern
choices.note: Lumo marks the plank with Questlight. Nothing unspools while you sit.

choices.label: Three more steps, then rest
choices.note: A short plan, then the same lantern. The bridge does not punish a pause.

choices.label: Stop right now
choices.note: Lumo nods. “Player one. Crew first. That includes you being finished.”

stories.reveal: A save point is a promise that the place will still be there. Leaving a quest is not losing it. Lumo used to think heroes never sat down. The bridge only opens for a crew that can choose to stop.
stories.activity: Invent a save-point signal for a real task: a bookmark, a sticker, or a word like “lantern”. Use it once this week when you want to pause without calling it quitting.
stories.grownup: The story welcomes a stop. If a child says they are done, treat that as information, not a hurdle to coach them past. It does not claim that breaks improve results.
stories.write: What would your save point look like?

stories.title: The Rumour Rune
stories.explore: Check the words before you believe a big claim.
stories.voice: That sounds huge. Let’s read the carving before we believe it.
stories.question: A whisper says the portal opens only for the fastest player. What should Lumo do?

choices.label: Read the rune together
choices.note: The carving is the source. The whisper is somebody’s version of it.

choices.label: Ask what a friend actually saw
choices.note: Nori remembers a different word. Two memories are a reason to look again.

choices.label: Try one slow step and watch
choices.note: A careful test. If the portal stays shut, the rumour still might be wrong.

stories.reveal: The rune says “Enter together.” The rumour dropped the last word and added “fastest”. Checking the carving changes the plan: the crew walks in side by side. A exciting story is not the same as the instruction.
stories.activity: Play missing-word. One person says a short rule and leaves a word out. The other finds what changed. Swap.
stories.grownup: This shows the difference between a retelling and a source. It is not a safety guarantee, and it does not teach a child to handle real rumours alone. Stay nearby for anything that matters.
stories.write: What would you want to check before you believed a big rumour?

stories.title: The Upside-Down Map
stories.explore: A thoughtful second look can be the brave part.
stories.voice: I announced the plan. Then I noticed the map was upside down. Second try?
stories.question: Sprout’s leaf-map was the wrong way up. Which move now?

choices.label: Turn it and look again
choices.note: The leaf arrows point the other way once the map is the right way up.

choices.label: Test the first path slowly
choices.note: One careful step. If the moss thins out, come back. That is still a plan.

choices.label: Ask what Nori notices
choices.note: A second pair of eyes. Sprout does not have to spot everything alone.

stories.reveal: The trail marks were leaves pointing toward the moss gate, not away from it. Sprout’s medal is for the second look. Traillight brightens when a plan gets repaired, not when it was perfect the first time.
stories.activity: Turn a drawing upside down and find one thing you missed. Then turn it back and tell someone what the second look found.
stories.grownup: Sprout celebrates a thoughtful retry instead of hiding the mix-up. Skip “you should have looked first.” The repair is the point. This does not promise fewer mistakes at school.
stories.write: Tell about a second try that helped — or invent one.

stories.title: Two Paths, One Puddle
stories.explore: You can choose a route, then switch.
stories.voice: New route. Same brave little feet. Which pattern first?
stories.question: A puddle sits across the path. How do we cross?

choices.label: Stepping stones
choices.note: Look at each stone before a boot goes down. Slippery is information.

choices.label: A leaf boat
choices.note: Small, silly, and only for a very shallow puddle. Name it if you like.

choices.label: The drier pebbles
choices.note: Nori points at a line of pebbles easy to miss. You may change your mind.

stories.reveal: Every choice can be a kind plan. The drier pebbles were there the whole time. Traillight marks the way you pick, and it does not sulk if you switch. Noticing is allowed to happen late.
stories.activity: On paper, draw a puddle and two ways around it. Circle the way that feels safest, and add one thing you would watch for.
stories.grownup: Practice is planning and revising, on paper. No real water is required. Switching is not failing the first idea.
stories.write: Which path would you pick, and what would you watch for?

stories.title: The Medal for Slow
stories.explore: Looking can matter more than being first.
stories.voice: I almost sprinted. The riddle wants the careful second attempt.
stories.question: The moss gate asks which footprint is the thoughtful one. What do you think?

choices.label: The fastest print
choices.note: Speed is a guess here. The gate does not open for it — and that is all right.

choices.label: The one that stopped to look
choices.note: A pause left a deeper print beside a tiny trail mark.

choices.label: The one that turned around
choices.note: Going back, then trying again, is still a footprint.

stories.reveal: The gate opens for the print that turned around. Sprout pins the medal on that second attempt. Fast was not wrong for every day. Today the riddle was about noticing. Traillight makes the medal glow emerald, then fades so nobody has to wear it.
stories.activity: Try a tiny task twice: once in a rush, once slower. Name one thing only the slower try noticed.
stories.grownup: The story values a second look. Don’t turn it into “fast is bad.” Some things are fine done quickly. Notice what the child actually spotted.
stories.write: What did a slower try notice?

stories.title: Weather Inside
stories.explore: A feeling does not have to be explained.
stories.voice: You don’t have to explain the sky. I can sit in it with you.
stories.question: A friend’s feeling is stormy, and they do not want to say why. What can Luna offer?

choices.label: Quiet company
choices.note: Sit nearby. No questions. Dreamlight stays low and steady.

choices.label: A story they can change
choices.note: Offer a tale. They may change the ending, or close the book.

choices.label: A drawing, no words
choices.note: Weather on paper. The reason can stay private.

stories.reveal: None of these asks “why”. Luna does not demand an explanation for a feeling. If words come later, there is room. If they don’t, company was the whole help. Dreamlight does not dim when a feeling stays unnamed.
stories.activity: If you want, draw today’s feeling as weather. You may keep the reason to yourself. Blank paper is a finished drawing too.
stories.grownup: Listening without requiring disclosure. If a child seems distressed, this page is not care — stay with them and use the support you already trust. It is not a treatment, and it does not reduce anxiety by itself.
stories.write: A weather word for right now, if you want one. Blank is welcome.

stories.title: The Library of Almosts
stories.explore: An unfinished idea can be enough.
stories.voice: An unfinished page is a door left kindly open.
stories.question: The sentence waiting on the shelf is “And then the moon…” How might it go?

choices.label: …lent us a lantern
choices.note: A borrowed light. Very polite of the moon.

choices.label: …waited while we thought
choices.note: No rush in the margin. The moon can hover.

choices.label: …asked nothing and glowed
choices.note: Some lights do not need a speech.

stories.reveal: All three endings are kind. Luna used to hide unfinished stories because they felt not-wonderful-enough. Dreamlight shows that a beginning can be the gift. Stopping is part of writing, not a hole in it.
stories.activity: Write one sentence and stop. You do not have to read it to anyone. You do not have to finish it tomorrow.
stories.grownup: Lowers the pressure to perform a perfect ending. Anything typed in the box below stays in the page only — it is not saved.
stories.write: Finish “And then the moon…” in your own way, or leave it almost.

stories.title: The Scarf Offer
stories.explore: Sharing a feeling is a choice.
stories.voice: Words are an invitation, not a test.
stories.question: Luna’s comet scarf can hold a feeling-word. Do you want to offer one?

choices.label: I’ll pick a word
choices.note: Any word. Luna does not grade it or ask you to explain it.

choices.label: Not today
choices.note: A complete answer. Luna nods and lets the scarf rest.

choices.label: A colour instead
choices.note: Violet, moss, gold, moon-blue, rose. A colour can be the whole reply.

stories.reveal: “Not today” does not need a follow-up question. Luna does not chase a feeling to make the story neat. Dreamlight stays soft either way. An invitation can be declined and still have been kind.
stories.activity: If you like, match three feelings to three colours. Skip any you would rather not name.
stories.grownup: Consent about sharing inner life. After this story, don’t quiz a child to “use their words.” Silence can be the respectful ending.
stories.write: A word, a colour, or nothing. The box does not mind.

stories.title: Lowbeam’s Offer
stories.explore: A calming idea can be declined.
stories.voice: We could notice three quiet things. And it might not help. That’s all right.
stories.question: Nori offers a quiet lantern activity. What do you want?

choices.label: Yes — three quiet things
choices.note: One you can see, one you can hear, one you can touch. Stop if you want.

choices.label: No — it doesn’t feel helpful
choices.note: Nori accepts that. Tidelight does not droop. The offer is over.

choices.label: Something else
choices.note: A sip of water, a stretch, or just sitting. Nori will follow your lead.

stories.reveal: A calming activity is an offer, not a rule. Nori used to think Lowbeam should always soothe. Some nights it doesn’t, and the friendship still holds. You can say no without owing a better idea.
stories.activity: Only if you want: name one thing you see, one you hear, and one you can touch. If that feels wrong, stop. Stopping is the activity working.
stories.grownup: Shows that a regulation idea is optional. Do not insist on breathing or noticing games. If worry is large, use real support — this is fiction, not a way to shrink anxiety.
stories.write: If you tried it: did it help, a little, or not at all? Every answer is allowed.

stories.title: Three Small Things
stories.voice: That pebble has a stripe like a tiny river. What else do you notice?
stories.question: The tidepool is full of tiny wonders. How do we look?

choices.label: A stripe or a mark
choices.note: Pick one pattern. You do not have to catalogue the whole pool.

choices.label: The quietest sound
choices.note: A drip, a sleeve, a far bird. Name one, then rest.

choices.label: One question, not ten
choices.note: Wonder about a single thing. Let the other questions wait.

stories.reveal: Nori once rehearsed a question so carefully that a beetle walked away. Tidelight prefers a small wonder, spoken in time. Three details, then one question, is a complete adventure.
stories.activity: With a grown-up if you leave the room, notice three tiny details on one cup, leaf or stone. Wonder about only one of them.
stories.grownup: Attention without a quiz at the end. Don’t ask them to report all three unless they offer. Curiosity here is shared, not marked.
stories.write: One small thing you noticed, and one question about it.

stories.title: The Trusted Door
stories.explore: Some questions belong with a person you trust.
stories.voice: Some questions are too big for a lantern. We can practise asking a person.
stories.question: Lowbeam cannot answer this one. Who could?

choices.label: A grown-up at home
choices.note: Nori helps with the sentence, not with the secret.

choices.label: A teacher or another adult you trust
choices.note: You choose the person. The story does not pick them for you.

choices.label: I’ll think, and not write a name
choices.note: Deciding privately still counts. The page does not need the name.

stories.reveal: A sentence you can borrow: “Can I tell you something that’s been sitting with me?” Nori does not ask what the something is. Heartlights are not people, and they are not a place for secrets. Asking someone you trust is the step that matters.
stories.activity: Practise the sentence with a toy if you want. Later, if it feels right, say it to a person you trust. You choose whether that happens.
stories.grownup: Rehearses help-seeking. The writing box is not stored and is not a report. If you are worried about a child’s safety, follow the safeguarding steps you already use. This story cannot detect harm or promise safety.
stories.write: You may practise the asking sentence. Do not write secrets. This box is not a person, and it is not saved.

stories.title: After the Drumroll
stories.voice: I tripped on my own entrance. I’m sorry. I’ll give you a little space.
stories.question: Moki apologised for the crash. What would feel okay?

choices.label: A bit of space
choices.note: Moki steps back and keeps the confetti in a pocket. The joke waits.

choices.label: A small laugh later
choices.note: Not now. Later, if you want it. Moki does not schedule the laugh.

choices.label: I accept — let’s fix the mess
choices.note: Pick up what fell. Fixing is allowed to be quiet.

stories.reveal: The apology comes before the joke. Space is a real choice, not a trick to hurry forgiveness. Sparklight stays in the room without crowding. Moki used to fill every silence. Today the silence is part of being kind.
stories.activity: Practise a short sorry you might actually use: what happened, that you are sorry, and one way to help. Then wait. Don’t add a joke unless the other person does.
stories.grownup: Models repair plus room. Don’t ask a child to forgive on a timer, and don’t turn the story into a script they must perform after every bump.
stories.write: What would “a little space” look like for you? You can skip this.

stories.title: Captain Teaspoon
stories.explore: A silly guess is useful once you check it.
stories.voice: Captain Teaspoon says triangles have four sides. Shall we check the captain’s maths?
stories.question: How do we check a claim that sounds funny?

choices.label: Count the sides
choices.note: Draw one and touch each side as you count. The drawing is the evidence.

choices.label: Ask what the word means
choices.note: “Tri” means three. The word itself is a clue, then the drawing checks it.

choices.label: Compare with four sides
choices.note: Draw a square too. Set them side by side. Different shapes, different counts.

stories.reveal: A triangle has three sides. Captain Teaspoon mixed it up with a square, which has four. The wrong guess was not embarrassing once it was checked. Oops. Plot twist. Sparklight likes the moment the idea gets corrected, kindly.
stories.activity: Draw a triangle and a square. Count the sides out loud. Then invent one wrong-on-purpose fact and correct it together.
stories.grownup: Separates a guess from a checked idea, in play. It is not a geometry test and does not say anything about a child’s school results.
stories.write: One wrong-on-purpose fact, then the checked fact.

stories.title: The Moon Behind the Cloud
stories.explore: A loud guess is not yet evidence.
stories.voice: I announced the moon was missing. Then I looked up properly.
stories.question: Moki says the moon is gone. What should we do before we agree?

choices.label: Wait and watch the cloud
choices.note: Clouds move. A minute of looking is a fair test.

choices.label: Ask what clouds do
choices.note: Nori has watched this before. A friend can be a source, then you still look.

choices.label: Check the other clues
choices.note: Stars are still there. The sky did not pack up. Something may be in the way.

stories.reveal: The moon was behind a cloud. Moki’s announcement was confident and unfinished. Evidence was the sky, watched for a little while. Sparklight and Tidelight check together. A missing moon did not need a rescue — it needed a second look.
stories.activity: Next time something seems to have vanished, list two other explanations before you decide it is gone. A sock, a pencil, a moon.
stories.grownup: Guess versus evidence, told as fiction. Enjoy the joke. Don’t turn every mix-up at home into a lesson.
stories.write: What else could explain a “missing” moon?
